The computational complexity of edit distance is one of the clearest examples of the difference between an algorithm that is easy to define and a problem whose true complexity remains remarkably subtle. The classical Levenshtein distance between two strings can be computed by a simple dynamic program in time proportional to the product of their lengths. More than half a century of research has produced important improvements, specialized algorithms, parameterized methods, bit-parallel implementations, approximation algorithms, and conditional lower bounds—but no general exact algorithm is known that breaks the quadratic barrier by a polynomial factor.

The familiar Levenshtein distance is one particularly important member of this family: insertion, deletion, and substitution are permitted, each with unit cost. But changing even one assumption produces a different mathematical object. Removing insertions and deletions gives Hamming distance. Removing substitution produces insertion-deletion distance and a direct relationship with longest common subsequences. Adding adjacent transposition leads toward Damerau–Levenshtein distance. Assigning nonuniform costs gives weighted edit distance. Changing gap costs produces sequence-alignment models. Normalizing the score changes its scale and can change its metric properties.
